result: Prior work (Corsa et al., 2016) demonstrated that DDR2 expression is increased in stromal cells of both primary breast tumors and lung metastases, and that DDR2 action in stromal cells of the recipient host regulates breast cancer lung metastases.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3 are all supported by citation to Corsa et al., 2016. These are background claims establishing prior knowledge that motivates the current study. The citation provides appropriate support for these foundational statements.

result: DDR2 action in stromal cells at the primary tumor site, rather than at the metastatic site, is critical for regulating breast cancer lung metastases. Tail vein injection experiments showed no difference in lung colonization between Ddr2+/+ and Ddr2-/- hosts, while orthotopic transplantation revealed decreased primary tumor volume and significantly reduced lung metastases in Ddr2-/- hosts.
evaluation: Claims C4-C7 are well-supported by experimental data in Figure 1. The tail vein injection experiment (C4) serves as a negative control showing DDR2 in the metastatic site is not critical, while the orthotopic transplant (C5-C6) demonstrates DDR2's importance at the primary site. The inference (C7) logically follows from these complementary experiments.

result: Prior work established that ubiquitous Ddr2-/- mice have altered collagen fiber organization in primary breast tumors that is more benign/less supportive of invasion, and these mice develop significantly reduced lung metastases.
evaluation: Claims C8-C10 are supported by citation to Corsa et al., 2016. These establish prior findings that motivate investigating the mechanism by which DDR2 controls collagen organization. C9 involves some interpretation but is appropriately attributed to prior work.

result: CAFs are the predominant stromal cell controlling ECM production and remodeling in tumors, and DDR2 expression is significantly upregulated in breast tumor CAFs during cancer progression.
evaluation: Claims C11-C12 are supported by appropriate citations (Bhowmick et al., 2004; Corsa et al., 2016; Gonzalez et al., 2017). These establish the rationale for focusing on CAFs as the key cell type to investigate DDR2 function.

result: DDR2 controls collagen matrix organization in cultured CAFs. WT CAFs produce ordered, linear collagen matrices while normal fibroblasts produce disorganized matrices. Ddr2-/- CAFs produce disorganized matrices similar to normal fibroblasts, and re-expression of WT DDR2 rescues the organized matrix phenotype.
evaluation: Claims C13-C15 are supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and citation to Corsa et al., 2016. The rescue experiment (C15) provides strong evidence that DDR2 is necessary and sufficient for this phenotype. This establishes a functional role for DDR2 in matrix organization.

result: Ddr2-/- CAFs exhibit decreased cell spreading on collagen I that requires DDR2 kinase activity for rescue, and show inhibited 3D collagen gel contraction compared to WT CAFs.
evaluation: Claims C16-C17 are supported by data in Figures 2A and 2—figure supplement 1D. The kinase-dead mutant control (C16) demonstrates that DDR2's catalytic activity is required. These phenotypes indicate altered mechanotransduction in Ddr2-/- CAFs.

result: DDR2-deficient CAFs form smaller focal adhesions on collagen I but not on fibronectin, with no change in focal adhesion number. The defect is rescued by WT DDR2 but not by collagen-binding defective DDR2.
evaluation: Claims C18-C21 are supported by data in Figures 2B-D and supplements. The fibronectin control (C19) demonstrates specificity for collagen, and the rescue with WT but not W52A mutant (C21) shows collagen binding is required. This indicates DDR2 specifically regulates collagen-dependent focal adhesion formation.

result: Ddr2-depleted CAFs exhibit dramatically reduced traction forces and diminished pMLC activity on collagen I. Both defects are rescued by WT DDR2 but not by collagen-binding defective DDR2.
evaluation: Claims C22-C25 are supported by data in Figures 2E and 2—figure supplement 2D. The traction force measurements provide functional evidence of altered mechanotransduction. The rescue experiments with mutants demonstrate both collagen binding and kinase activity are required.

result: DDR2-deficient mouse and human breast CAFs exhibit altered mechanotransduction activity when plated on or in collagen I.
evaluation: Claim C26 is a summary inference supported by the collective evidence from C16-C25. Multiple independent assays (spreading, gel contraction, focal adhesions, traction forces, pMLC) all demonstrate mechanotransduction defects in Ddr2-deficient CAFs.

result: DDR2 depletion reduces active β1 integrin-Talin1 and Kindlin2 co-localization at cell protrusions without affecting total β1 integrin or Talin1 levels. Co-immunoprecipitation confirms reduced β1 integrin-Talin1 interaction in Ddr2-depleted CAFs on collagen I.
evaluation: Claims C28-C32 are supported by data in Figures 3A-D and supplements. The super-resolution microscopy provides spatial resolution of protein localization, while Western blots and co-IP provide biochemical confirmation. The finding that total protein levels are unchanged (C30-C31) but interactions are reduced indicates DDR2 regulates integrin activation rather than expression.

result: DDR2 depletion does not affect β1 integrin activation or focal adhesion size on fibronectin, demonstrating specificity for collagen-binding integrins.
evaluation: Claims C33-C34 are supported by data in Figures 3E and 2—figure supplement 2B-C. These negative controls are critical for demonstrating that DDR2 specifically regulates collagen-binding integrins rather than all β1-containing integrins. This specificity strengthens the mechanistic model.

result: DDR2 in CAFs influences full activation of collagen-binding integrins at adhesive sites by controlling Talin1 and Kindlin2 activation and/or recruitment to integrin complexes in cell protrusions.
evaluation: Claim C35 is a mechanistic inference supported by the collective evidence from C28-C34. The data demonstrate reduced Talin1 and Kindlin2 co-localization with active integrins without changes in total protein levels, supporting the proposed mechanism of regulating recruitment/activation rather than expression.

result: DDR2 does not colocalize with β1 integrin at adhesive sites within cell protrusions, as measured by Pearson's correlation coefficient.
evaluation: Claim C36 is supported by super-resolution microscopy data in Figure 4A. This negative result is important for ruling out direct DDR2-integrin complex formation and supports an indirect signaling mechanism. The quantitative Pearson's coefficient provides objective measurement.

result: Collagen I exposure activates RAP1 in WT CAFs. Ddr2-depleted CAFs have less total RAP1 and significantly reduced RAP1 activation after collagen I exposure.
evaluation: Claims C37-C39 are supported by RAP1-GTP pulldown data in Figure 4B. The quantification accounts for differences in total RAP1 levels (C38), strengthening the conclusion about reduced activation (C39). This identifies RAP1 as a key intermediate in DDR2 signaling to integrins.

result: Constitutively active RAP1 (V12 and Q63E mutants) and forskolin treatment rescue β1 integrin surface activation and Talin1 recruitment in Ddr2-depleted CAFs.
evaluation: Claims C40-C41 are supported by super-resolution microscopy data in Figures 4C and 4—figure supplement 1B. These rescue experiments provide strong evidence that RAP1 acts downstream of DDR2 and is sufficient to restore integrin activation. The use of two different RAP1 mutants and an independent activator (forskolin) strengthens the conclusion.

result: Following collagen I exposure, DDR2 activation leads to upregulation of RAP1 activity, which enhances Talin1 activation and recruitment to integrin complexes in cellular protrusions and subsequent full activation of collagen-binding β1 integrins.
evaluation: Claim C42 is a mechanistic model supported by the collective evidence from C37-C41. The data demonstrate: (1) DDR2 is required for RAP1 activation, (2) RAP1 activation is sufficient to rescue integrin activation and Talin1 recruitment, and (3) this pathway is specific to collagen. This establishes a clear DDR2→RAP1→Talin1→integrin signaling axis.

result: FSP1cre is expressed in 75% of breast tumor CAFs (FAP+ cells) and 90% of CD45+ leukocytes, but not in tumor epithelial cells (K8+, K14+) or endothelial cells (CD31+).
evaluation: Claims C43-C45 are supported by lineage tracing data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A. This characterization is critical for interpreting the FSP1cre deletion experiments. The authors appropriately acknowledge the lack of CAF specificity (C45), which is an important limitation for interpretation.

result: In FSP1cre; Ddr2fl/fl; MMTV-PyMT mice, the Ddr2 gene is rearranged in whole tumors and DDR2 protein is not expressed in isolated CAFs.
evaluation: Claims C46-C47 are supported by DNA genotyping (Figure 5A) and Western blot (Figure 5B) data. These confirm successful Ddr2 deletion in CAFs, validating the genetic model. The partial rearrangement in whole tumors (C46) is expected given that not all cells express FSP1cre.

result: FSP1cre-mediated deletion of Ddr2 significantly reduces lung metastases without affecting primary tumor burden, latency, or CAF numbers.
evaluation: Claims C48-C49 are supported by data in Figures 5C-F. The selective effect on metastasis without affecting primary tumor growth or CAF numbers suggests DDR2 in CAFs specifically regulates the metastatic process rather than tumor growth or CAF recruitment. This is a key phenotypic finding.

result: Ddr2-/- FSP1cre tumors show no difference in overall collagen content but have altered collagen fiber architecture: fibers are curlier, shorter, and thinner. There is increased TACS1 (benign) signature and decreased TACS3 (aggressive) signature compared to WT tumors.
evaluation: Claims C50-C54 are supported by picosirius red staining (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) and SHG imaging (Figures 5G-H). The finding that total collagen is unchanged but organization is altered (C50-C51) indicates DDR2 regulates matrix remodeling rather than production. The TACS analysis provides clinical relevance by linking to established prognostic signatures.

result: FIB-SEM analysis reveals that within 2-5 microns of the tumor-stromal boundary, Ddr2-deficient tumors have less collagen with significantly thinner and more fragmented fibers.
evaluation: Claim C55 is supported by FIB-SEM data in Figures 5I-J and Videos 1-3. This high-resolution 3D imaging provides detailed structural information about collagen organization at the critical tumor-stromal interface. The quantification of fiber width strengthens the conclusion.

result: Ddr2-/- FSP1cre tumors are significantly less stiff overall, with stiffness changes specifically at the tumor-stromal boundary. This correlates with reduced pMLC activity in tumor slices.
evaluation: Claims C56-C58 are supported by AFM measurements (Figures 6A-D) and pMLC staining (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C). The spatial specificity of stiffness changes at the tumor-stromal boundary (C57) is particularly important as this is where invasion occurs. The correlation with pMLC activity provides a cellular mechanism.

result: In tumor organoids embedded in collagen I, active β1 integrin is abundant in both CAFs and tumor cells in WT organoids. In Ddr2-/- FSP1cre organoids, active β1 integrin is decreased in CAFs but unchanged in tumor cells. In ubiquitous Ddr2-/- organoids, active β1 integrin is decreased in both cell types.
evaluation: Claims C59-C62 are supported by tumor organoid data in Figures 7A-E. This ex vivo system bridges the gap between cultured cells and intact tumors. The cell-type specific effects in FSP1cre vs ubiquitous deletion (C60-C61) demonstrate DDR2 acts cell-autonomously to regulate integrin activation in vivo.

result: DDR2 in CAFs is a critical regulator of breast tumor ECM collagen fiber organization and tumor stiffness. FSP1cre-mediated Ddr2 deletion results in reduced stiffness and altered collagen organization at the tumor-stromal boundary, associated with decreased lung metastases.
evaluation: Claims C63-C65 synthesize the major in vivo findings from C48-C58. The data demonstrate DDR2 in CAFs controls: (1) collagen fiber organization, (2) tumor stiffness, and (3) metastasis. The association between these phenotypes (C65) is correlative but supported by the mechanistic data linking DDR2 to mechanotransduction.

result: DDR2 in CAFs controls mechanotransduction and full activation of collagen-binding β1 integrins via RAP1-mediated Talin1 and Kindlin2 recruitment. This occurs in cultured CAFs and in CAFs and tumor cells within primary tumors in vivo.
evaluation: Claims C66-C70 synthesize the major mechanistic findings. The evidence spans multiple experimental systems (isolated CAFs, tumor organoids) and includes loss-of-function, rescue, and mutant analyses. The pathway DDR2→RAP1→Talin1/Kindlin2→integrin activation is well-supported by the data.

result: DDR2 in CAFs affects mRNA expression of collagen genes and collagen-modifying enzymes such as lysyl oxidases and MMPs.
evaluation: Claim C71 is supported by citation to Corsa et al., 2016. This establishes that DDR2 has multiple mechanisms of action beyond integrin regulation. However, no new data on gene expression is presented in the current study.

result: FIB-SEM reveals less and thinner collagen at the tumor-stromal interface in Ddr2-deficient tumors, while trichrome/Sirius red staining shows no difference. SHG analysis detects changes in collagen structure similar to FIB-SEM.
evaluation: Claims C72-C74 are supported by comparing different imaging modalities. The discrepancy between FIB-SEM/SHG (detecting changes) and histologic staining (no changes) suggests the alterations are subtle and require high-resolution or specialized imaging. This highlights the importance of method selection for detecting matrix changes.

result: FSP1cre is expressed in both CAFs and CD45+ myeloid cells. However, ubiquitous Ddr2-/- tumors show no differences in immune cell numbers compared to WT.
evaluation: Claims C75-C76 address a potential confound. C75 acknowledges the limitation of FSP1cre specificity (supported by lineage tracing data). C76 (supported by citation to Corsa et al., 2016) suggests immune cells may not be the primary driver of the phenotype, though this doesn't definitively rule out their contribution.

result: Deletion of Ddr2 in breast epithelial cells only (MMTV-Cre or K14-Cre) does not affect primary tumor matrix production or organization.
evaluation: Claim C77 is supported by citation to Corsa et al., 2016. This control experiment rules out tumor cell-intrinsic effects of DDR2 on matrix organization, supporting the conclusion that CAF-expressed DDR2 is the critical regulator.

result: Super-resolution microscopy and co-immunoprecipitation experiments found no evidence that DDR2 and collagen-binding integrins form complexes in cells.
evaluation: Claim C78 is supported by experimental data (referenced in text). This negative result is important for the mechanistic model, ruling out direct DDR2-integrin interaction and supporting an indirect signaling mechanism via RAP1.

result: Prior work showed that DDR2 overexpression in HEK293 cells increases α1β1 and α2β1 integrin affinity without affecting surface levels, and that endogenous DDR2 is upregulated in CAFs during breast cancer progression and is critical for their activation.
evaluation: Claims C79-C80 are supported by appropriate citations. These establish prior observations that motivated the current mechanistic investigation. C79 provides precedent for DDR2 regulating integrin affinity, while C80 establishes the biological relevance in CAFs.

result: DDR2 in breast tumor CAFs controls collagen-binding integrin activation by activating RAP1 to regulate Talin1 and Kindlin2 recruitment. Inside-out RAP1 signaling regulating Talin1-mediated integrin activation is well-established in hematopoietic cells, and the current work demonstrates functional consequences in mesenchymal cells and tumor progression in vivo.
evaluation: Claims C81-C83 synthesize the mechanistic findings and place them in context of prior work. C81 summarizes the pathway established by the current data. C82 (supported by citations) provides precedent from other cell types. C83 highlights the novelty of demonstrating this pathway in CAFs and its functional importance in vivo.

result: Most defective mechanobiologic properties of Ddr2-/- CAFs are likely manifestations of defective collagen-binding β1 integrin activity rather than other DDR2 signaling pathways.
evaluation: Claim C84 is an interpretive statement supported by the collective evidence. The rescue experiments with constitutively active RAP1 (restoring integrin activation and multiple mechanotransduction phenotypes) support this interpretation. However, the authors appropriately use cautious language ('likely') acknowledging other pathways may contribute.

result: DDR2 also regulates SNAIL1, a critical regulator of fibrogenic responses in CAFs. Mechanical signals regulate SNAIL1 levels and function. Overall tumor matrix organization controlled by DDR2 likely involves both integrin regulation and SNAIL1.
evaluation: Claims C85-C88 are supported by appropriate citations. These establish that DDR2 has multiple downstream pathways. C88 is a reasonable inference that both pathways contribute, though the current study focuses on the integrin pathway. This acknowledges complexity without overinterpreting the data.

result: DDR2 activation by collagen is slow (hours) and sustained. DDR2 signals stabilizing SNAIL1 take 4-6 hours, while DDR2 regulation of β1 integrin occurs within 15-30 minutes but requires kinase activity. This suggests distinct signaling pathways to RAP1/integrin versus SNAIL1.
evaluation: Claims C89-C92 are supported by citations (C89-C90) and experimental data (C91). The kinetic differences (C91 vs C90) support the inference of distinct pathways (C92). This temporal analysis provides insight into signaling architecture, though C92 appropriately uses cautious language ('could be distinct').

result: DDR2 in CAFs is a critical pathway controlling tumor-permissive ECM that facilitates invasion and metastasis. Inside-out regulation of collagen-binding integrins occurs in mesenchymal cells in vivo with significant impact on cancer progression. DDR2 could represent a therapeutic target for preventing metastasis.
evaluation: Claims C93-C94 are well-supported by the collective evidence from the study. C95 is appropriately speculative ('could represent') and follows logically from the findings. The therapeutic potential is reasonable given the demonstrated role in metastasis, though clinical validation would be required.

result: DDR2 action in tissue fibroblasts may contribute to other organ fibrosis pathologies in response to injury or inflammation.
evaluation: Claim C96 is appropriately speculative and supported by citations to fibrosis literature. This suggests broader implications beyond cancer, which is reasonable given the fundamental role of DDR2 in fibroblast mechanotransduction. However, this remains to be tested experimentally.

result: The study demonstrates that DDR2 in CAFs influences mechanotransduction by controlling collagen-binding integrin activation via Rap1-mediated Talin1 and Kindlin2 recruitment. This is critical for remodeling collagen fibers at the tumor-stromal boundary to generate a physically permissive microenvironment for invasion and metastasis.
evaluation: Claims C97-C100 summarize the major findings and conclusions. C97-C98 establish the biological context (supported by general knowledge). C99-C100 synthesize the key mechanistic and functional findings, which are well-supported by the experimental data throughout the study.

result: Background on tumor stiffness and collagen in breast cancer: Increased tumor stiffness influences multiple cellular processes. Collagen fiber production and remodeling are major contributors to tumor stiffness. In breast tumors, collagen characteristics differ from normal tissue. Dense breasts have increased cancer risk. Collagen fiber organization affects tumor mechanics and metastasis. TACS signatures correlate with tumor aggressiveness.
evaluation: Claims C101-C109 provide background context supported by appropriate citations. These establish the biological and clinical significance of the research question. The claims draw from established literature and provide motivation for the study.

result: Background on CAFs: CAFs are the major effector cells responsible for ECM production and remodeling in tumors. They remodel stroma through enzyme secretion and force-mediated mechanisms. Other cell types can also impact ECM remodeling directly or indirectly.
evaluation: Claims C110-C112 provide background on CAF biology supported by appropriate citations. These establish why CAFs are the focus of the study and acknowledge the complexity of the tumor microenvironment.

result: Background on DDR2: Prior work in GEMMs and transplant models showed DDR2 in tumor and stromal cells regulates breast cancer metastasis. DDR2 is not expressed in normal breast epithelium but is induced in 50-70% of invasive breast tumors and correlates with poor outcomes. DDR2 is an unusual RTK with collagen as its ligand and slow activation kinetics. It may affect integrin affinity.
evaluation: Claims C113-C120 provide background on DDR2 supported by appropriate citations. These establish what is known about DDR2 in breast cancer and its unusual properties as an RTK. C120 specifically motivates the investigation of DDR2-integrin interactions.

result: Background on integrins: Integrins are critical for cancer development and metastasis. In GEMMs, Ddr2 deletion has greater impact on metastasis than α1 or α2 integrin deletion, while β1 integrin is critical for tumor initiation. DDR2 and integrins have distinct collagen binding sites, and DDR2 can be activated independently of integrins.
evaluation: Claims C121-C125 provide background on integrins and their relationship to DDR2, supported by appropriate citations. These establish the importance of integrins in cancer and the potential for DDR2-integrin crosstalk without direct interaction.

result: Background on integrin function: Integrins are adhesion molecules and signaling receptors with major functions in mechanosensing and mechanotransduction, making them sensitive to mechanical properties of the cellular environment.
evaluation: Claims C126-C128 provide background on integrin function supported by appropriate citations. These establish why integrins are logical candidates for mediating DDR2's effects on mechanotransduction.

result: Summary of key findings: Genetic deletion of Ddr2 in breast tumor CAFs impacts mechanotransduction properties. DDR2 is selectively required for full activation of collagen-binding integrins (fibronectin-activated integrins are normal). In vivo, Ddr2 deletion in CAFs results in less stiff tumors with altered collagen organization at the tumor-stromal boundary and decreased β1 integrin activity.
evaluation: Claims C129-C131 summarize the major findings of the study. These are well-supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript and represent the key conclusions.
